control_results.control_name: Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets
control_results.score_rationale: The policy assigns responsibility for maintaining asset and system inventories to PO Executives and defines roles for oversight, but lacks a detailed, formalized process for actively discovering, tracking, and correcting all enterprise assets across physical, virtual, remote, and cloud environments.
evidence: Maintains an up-to-date listing of the information systems and assets, and information (data) under their control and maintains awareness of the cybersecurity risk posture of each information system;

Ensures current system inventories, system-level security plans, security reviews, corrective action plans, security authorization packages, and similar cybersecurity documents are developed, maintained, and posted to ED's system of record for FISMA reporting.

Ensures that a PO-level asset, data, and information security continuous monitoring strategy is developed and implemented to enable ongoing visibility into the cybersecurity risk posture of each information system within the PO;
Manages personnel, assets, data, and information, and physical security matters within the PO;
gaps: No defined process or tooling for automated discovery of enterprise assets across physical, virtual, remote, and cloud environments.
No mention of a centralized, authoritative enterprise asset inventory or configuration management database (CMDB) that consolidates all asset types.
No specific procedures for identifying and remediating unauthorized or unmanaged assets connected to the network.
No defined frequency or cadence for asset inventory updates, reconciliation, or validation.
No coverage of asset types beyond information systems (e.g., endpoints, IoT devices, BYOD, network infrastructure, cloud instances).
No defined metrics or accountability mechanisms for measuring completeness and accuracy of the asset inventory.
recommendations: Implement an enterprise-wide asset management policy that mandates automated discovery and inventory of all asset types—physical, virtual, remote, and cloud-based—using dedicated tools (e.g., network scanning, agent-based discovery, cloud API integration).

Establish a centralized asset inventory repository (CMDB) with mandatory fields including asset owner, location, classification, and network connectivity status, and integrate it with existing systems like CSAM.
Define a regular cadence (e.g., at least weekly automated scans, monthly reconciliation) for asset inventory updates and validation against network-connected devices.
Develop a process to identify, investigate, and remediate unauthorized assets detected on the network, with defined escalation timelines and responsible parties.
Establish KPIs and reporting metrics for asset inventory completeness and accuracy, with regular reporting to the CISO and senior leadership.

control_results.control_name: Inventory and Control of Software Assets
control_results.score_rationale: The policy addresses general asset inventory and continuous monitoring responsibilities but does not specifically address software asset inventory, authorized software lists (whitelisting), or mechanisms to prevent unauthorized software installation and execution.
evidence: Maintains an up-to-date listing of the information systems and assets, and information (data) under their control and maintains awareness of the cybersecurity risk posture of each information system

Ensures current system inventories, system-level security plans, security reviews, corrective action plans, security authorization packages, and similar cybersecurity documents are developed, maintained, and posted to ED's system of record for FISMA reporting

Ensures continuous monitoring of the information system's security is performed and validates the information system against the System Security Plan (SSP) while managing and controlling any information system updates
gaps: No explicit requirement for maintaining a comprehensive inventory of all authorized software assets across the network
No application whitelisting or software execution control policy to prevent unauthorized software from running
No defined process for discovering, identifying, and removing unauthorized or unmanaged software
No mention of software asset management tools, automated discovery mechanisms, or software catalogs
No policy addressing control of software installation privileges or software approval workflows
System-level asset inventory is mentioned but is not differentiated to include software-specific inventory requirements
recommendations: Develop and implement a formal software asset inventory policy that requires maintaining a complete, up-to-date catalog of all authorized software, including version information, across all network-connected devices
Implement application whitelisting controls that restrict software execution to only pre-approved applications and define a formal software approval and request process
Deploy automated software discovery and inventory tools that continuously scan the network to identify unauthorized or unmanaged software installations
Establish a formal process for periodic review and reconciliation of installed software against the authorized software inventory, with defined remediation timelines for unauthorized software
Define clear roles and responsibilities for software asset management, including who approves new software, who maintains the inventory, and who enforces compliance
Integrate software asset management metrics into continuous monitoring and FISMA reporting processes to track compliance over time

control_results.score_rationale: The policy contains scattered references to data protection, PII handling, privacy impact assessments, and disposal of SPII/PII, but lacks formal, comprehensive processes for data classification, data loss prevention (DLP), encryption controls, data retention schedules, and secure data disposal beyond PII. The coverage is ad hoc and privacy-focused rather than addressing the full scope of CIS Control 3.
evidence: Reviews and approves all ED Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs) Privacy Threshold Analyses (PTA)s and System of Records Notices (SORNs)
ensure compliance with all applicable laws and regulations regarding the collection, use, maintenance, sharing, protecting, and disposal of SPII and PII
Shares only the minimum PII from ED systems and applications that is necessary and relevant for the purposes it was originally collected
Authorized user access must be limited to only information necessary for the performance of required tasks
Ensures ED systems or applications that currently disseminate data for any purpose are capable of extracting data by pre-approved categories
gaps: No formal data classification scheme or process for identifying and classifying all data types (not just PII/SPII)
No data loss prevention (DLP) technical controls or processes defined
No encryption requirements or standards specified for data at rest or in transit
No comprehensive data retention policy with defined retention schedules
No formal secure data disposal procedures beyond general mention of PII disposal
No data handling procedures covering the full data lifecycle for all sensitivity levels
No data inventory or data flow mapping processes described
recommendations: Develop and document a formal data classification policy that categorizes all organizational data (not just PII) into defined sensitivity levels with corresponding handling requirements
Implement and document data loss prevention (DLP) controls at network boundaries, endpoints, and cloud services with monitoring and alerting capabilities
Define and enforce encryption standards for data at rest and in transit, specifying approved algorithms, key management procedures, and minimum encryption requirements by data classification level
Establish a comprehensive data retention schedule that specifies retention periods for each data category and the legal/regulatory basis for retention
Develop formal secure data disposal and sanitization procedures aligned with NIST SP 800-88, covering all media types and data classifications
Create a data inventory and data flow mapping process to identify where sensitive data resides, how it moves, and what protections are applied at each stage

control_results.control_name: Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets and Software
control_results.score_rationale: The policy contains several elements related to secure configuration—such as patch management, security control integration during system development, vulnerability patching timelines, and references to NIST SP 800-53—but lacks explicit mention of hardening guides, baseline configurations, configuration management databases, or formal secure configuration standards for enterprise assets and software.
evidence: Implements proper system backups and patch management processes

Ensures the requirements are effectively integrated into IT component products and information systems through purposeful security architecting, design, development, and configuration, following the ED change management processes
Ensures that actions are taken to respond and complies within specified timelines for any government-wide or ED-wide directed action items related to vulnerability patching
Assesses the performance of security and privacy controls associated with the system/network or web service to ensure the residual risk is maintained within an acceptable range

Identifies, tailors, documents, and implements information security and privacy-related functional requirements necessary to protect ED information, information systems, missions, and business processes
gaps: No explicit requirement to establish and maintain secure configuration baselines or hardening guides (e.g., CIS Benchmarks, DISA STIGs) for enterprise assets and software
No mention of a configuration management database (CMDB) or centralized tracking of approved configurations
No defined process for periodic review and validation of secure configurations against established baselines
No specific policy language addressing default credential removal, disabling unnecessary services/ports, or other standard hardening practices
No metrics or monitoring mechanisms defined for configuration drift detection and remediation
recommendations: Develop and formally document secure configuration baselines for all enterprise asset categories (servers, endpoints, network devices, mobile devices) referencing industry hardening guides such as CIS Benchmarks or DISA STIGs
Implement a configuration management process that includes a CMDB, automated configuration drift detection, and defined remediation timelines
Establish a policy requirement for periodic (at least quarterly) review and validation of system configurations against approved baselines
Define specific hardening requirements including removal of default credentials, disabling unnecessary services and protocols, and enforcing least-functionality principles
Integrate configuration compliance metrics into existing FISMA reporting and continuous monitoring programs to enable measured and monitored accountability

control_results.score_rationale: The policy formally defines processes for assigning and managing authorization to user accounts, including determining access rights based on least privilege, conducting quarterly account reviews, enforcing separation of duties, and distinguishing between privileged and non-privileged account usage. However, it lacks specific coverage of service account management, automated tooling for account lifecycle management, and defined metrics for monitoring account management effectiveness.
evidence: Determines who should be granted access to the system and with what rights and privileges, and grants users the fewest possible privileges necessary for job performance in order to ensure privileges are based on a legitimate need;
Conducts quarterly reviews and validations of system users' accounts to ensure the continued need for access to a system;
Enforces the concept of separation of duties by ensuring that no single individual has control of the entirety of any critical process in coordination with the ISSO;
Uses non-privileged accounts or roles when accessing non-security functions, and; Prevents non-privileged users from executing privileged functions and audit the execution of such function.
utilize PIV based authentication approaches
gaps: No explicit mention of service account management processes (creation, monitoring, credential rotation, lifecycle management)
No defined process or tooling for automated account provisioning and deprovisioning
No specific policy for managing shared or group accounts
No defined metrics or KPIs for measuring the effectiveness of account management processes
No explicit account disabling/removal procedures for terminated or transferred personnel
No mention of centralized account inventory or asset-to-account mapping for enterprise assets and software
recommendations: Develop and document explicit policies and procedures for service account lifecycle management, including creation, credential rotation, monitoring, and decommissioning
Implement automated account provisioning and deprovisioning tools integrated with HR systems to ensure timely access changes upon personnel transitions
Establish a centralized account inventory that maps all user, administrator, and service accounts to enterprise assets and software
Define measurable KPIs for account management (e.g., time to deprovision, percentage of orphaned accounts, timeliness of quarterly reviews) and report on them regularly
Add explicit procedures for disabling or removing accounts upon employee termination, transfer, or role change within defined timeframes
Document policies governing shared and group accounts, including restrictions on their use and enhanced monitoring requirements

control_results.score_rationale: The policy formally documents several key access control management processes including least privilege assignment, quarterly account reviews, separation of duties, privileged user responsibilities, and PIV-based authentication requirements. However, it lacks explicit coverage of full credential lifecycle management (creation, revocation), service account management, and automated tooling for access provisioning.
evidence: Determines who should be granted access to the system and with what rights and privileges, and grants users the fewest possible privileges necessary for job performance in order to ensure privileges are based on a legitimate need;
Conducts quarterly reviews and validations of system users' accounts to ensure the continued need for access to a system;
Enforces the concept of separation of duties by ensuring that no single individual has control of the entirety of any critical process in coordination with the ISSO;
Uses non-privileged accounts or roles when accessing non-security functions, and; Prevents non-privileged users from executing privileged functions and audit the execution of such function.
a privileged user is any user that has sufficient access rights to modify, including disabling, controls that are in place to protect the system.

Ensures that all IT systems under their purview are configured in accordance with most recent ED and Federal system security configuration guidance, and Federal CIO Council guidance (e.g., OMB M-11-11 and the Federal Identity Credential and Access Management Roadmap and Implementation Guidance);

Initiates and monitors background investigations and ensure that all users on their contracts comply with Federal and ED guidance for personnel security and background investigation requirements, and have taken security and awareness training before granting access to ED's systems and information;
gaps: No explicit process for creating and provisioning user, administrator, and service account credentials
No defined process for revoking access credentials upon role change, termination, or contract end
No mention of service account management (creation, assignment, monitoring, revocation)
No reference to specific tools or automated systems used for access control management and provisioning
No defined metrics or KPIs for measuring the effectiveness of access control management beyond quarterly reviews
No explicit policy on password/credential management standards (complexity, rotation, expiration)
recommendations: Develop and document a complete credential lifecycle management process covering creation, assignment, modification, and revocation for all account types (user, administrator, service accounts)
Implement and document specific tooling for centralized access provisioning, de-provisioning, and access certification (e.g., an Identity Governance and Administration platform)
Establish formal offboarding/role-change procedures that include timely revocation of access credentials and privileges
Create a dedicated service account management policy that addresses creation, ownership, periodic review, and credential rotation for service and application accounts
Define measurable metrics for access control management effectiveness, such as time-to-provision, time-to-revoke, percentage of orphaned accounts, and review completion rates
Document password and credential management standards including complexity requirements, rotation schedules, and multi-factor authentication requirements beyond PIV

control_results.score_rationale: The policy addresses several elements of vulnerability management including patch installation timelines, compliance with DHS Binding Operational Directives, POA&M tracking of weaknesses, and continuous monitoring strategies, but it lacks a formal, comprehensive vulnerability management plan with defined scanning cadences, prioritization criteria, remediation SLAs, and metrics for tracking the window of exposure.
evidence: Ensures that security patches for all assigned information systems are installed within the timeframe identified by ED policy

In support of the ISO, ensures that actions are taken to respond and comply within specified timelines for any government-wide or ED-wide directed action items related to vulnerability patching; This includes actions directed by the DHS, which issues "Binding Operational Directives" (BODs), that mandate reporting requirements by the Department for remediating critical vulnerabilities
Ensures that information security notices and advisories are distributed to appropriate ED and contractor personnel and that vendor-issued security patches are expeditiously installed

Assists their applicable System Owner in capturing all system weaknesses, policy and standard deviations in the POA&M and entering them into the Department's selected central cybersecurity repository (currently CSAM)

Ensures that a PO-level asset, data, and information security continuous monitoring strategy is developed and implemented to enable ongoing visibility into the cybersecurity risk posture of each information system within the PO

Ensures continuous monitoring of the information system's security is performed and validates the information system against the System Security Plan (SSP) while managing and controlling any information system updates
gaps: No defined vulnerability scanning plan specifying tools, frequency, scope, and coverage of all enterprise assets
No explicit vulnerability prioritization methodology or risk-based remediation criteria (e.g., CVSS-based severity thresholds)
No defined remediation SLAs or specific timeframes for different vulnerability severity levels beyond general references to 'ED policy' timelines
No mention of automated vulnerability scanning tools or integration with asset inventory for continuous assessment
No defined metrics or KPIs for measuring vulnerability management effectiveness (e.g., mean time to remediate, percentage of assets scanned, aging of vulnerabilities)
No process for validating remediation or rescanning after patches are applied
No mention of vulnerability assessment for non-traditional assets such as cloud, containers, or mobile devices
recommendations: Develop a formal Continuous Vulnerability Management Plan that defines scanning frequency (e.g., authenticated scans at least weekly for critical assets), tools, and scope covering all enterprise assets
Establish risk-based remediation SLAs with specific timeframes tied to vulnerability severity (e.g., critical within 15 days, high within 30 days, medium within 90 days)
Implement automated vulnerability scanning integrated with the enterprise asset inventory to ensure complete coverage and continuous assessment
Define and track vulnerability management metrics such as mean time to remediate, scan coverage percentage, and vulnerability aging, with regular reporting to leadership
Establish a formal rescanning/validation process to confirm that remediated vulnerabilities have been effectively addressed
Create a vulnerability prioritization framework that considers exploitability, asset criticality, and threat intelligence to focus remediation efforts

control_results.score_rationale: The policy contains indirect references to monitoring, continuous monitoring, and incident response that peripherally relate to audit log management, but there is no formal, documented audit log management process addressing collection, alerting, review, or retention of audit logs as specifically required by CIS-8.
evidence: Aligns the FSA cybersecurity operations center capabilities to actively monitor and respond to FSA related cyber incidents in coordination with the EDSOC.

Ensures continuous monitoring of the information system's security is performed and validates the information system against the System Security Plan (SSP) while managing and controlling any information system updates

Ensures that a PO-level asset, data, and information security continuous monitoring strategy is developed and implemented to enable ongoing visibility into the cybersecurity risk posture of each information system within the PO
Follows the guidance found in ED's Common Controls Catalog and the current version of NIST SP 800-53, reviewing at least annually
gaps: No defined audit log management process (collection, review, retention, and disposal)
No specification of which events or log types must be collected across systems
No defined alerting mechanisms or thresholds for audit log anomalies
No audit log retention requirements or retention periods specified
No requirements for centralized log aggregation or SIEM integration
No defined roles or responsibilities specifically for audit log review and management
No mention of protecting audit logs from unauthorized access, modification, or deletion
No periodic review cadence established for audit log analysis
recommendations: Develop and publish a formal Audit Log Management Policy that defines what events must be logged, how logs are collected, stored, reviewed, and retained
Specify minimum log retention periods aligned with regulatory and organizational requirements (e.g., 90 days online, 1 year archived)
Define specific event types that must be logged (e.g., authentication events, privilege escalation, configuration changes, access to sensitive data)

Assign explicit responsibilities for audit log review to ISSOs or SOC personnel with defined review frequencies
Establish controls to ensure audit log integrity and protection against tampering or unauthorized deletion

control_results.score_rationale: The policy document contains no specific provisions addressing email and web browser protections, threat detection for email/web vectors, or controls to mitigate risks from phishing, malicious URLs, or browser-based attacks. The excerpts only show general cybersecurity policy framing and reference lists without any substantive email or web browser security controls.
gaps: No email security controls defined (e.g., SPF, DKIM, DMARC, anti-phishing, anti-spam, attachment sandboxing)
No web browser hardening or protection requirements (e.g., approved browser configurations, URL filtering, blocking unauthorized browser extensions/plugins)
No mention of web content filtering or proxy-based protections
No requirements for DNS-based filtering or blocking of known malicious domains
No policies addressing protection against malicious email attachments or links
No user awareness training requirements specifically targeting email and web-based threats
No network-level email protections such as email gateway security or encryption requirements for email in transit
recommendations: Develop and document a comprehensive email security policy requiring SPF, DKIM, and DMARC implementation, anti-phishing controls, attachment scanning/sandboxing, and URL rewriting/inspection
Establish web browser hardening standards including approved browsers, automatic update requirements, restriction of unauthorized extensions/plugins, and secure default configurations
Implement and document requirements for URL/web content filtering to block access to known malicious or unauthorized categories of websites
Define DNS-based protections (e.g., DNS sinkholing, protective DNS services) to prevent connections to malicious domains
Integrate email and web browser threat metrics into continuous monitoring and incident response processes
Require periodic phishing simulation exercises and targeted security awareness training focused on email and web-based social engineering threats

control_results.score_rationale: The policy contains no specific provisions for malware defenses such as anti-malware software, endpoint detection, application whitelisting, or automated malicious code prevention. There are only tangential references to patching, continuous monitoring, and general cybersecurity responsibilities that indirectly relate to malware defense.
evidence: Ensures that security patches for all assigned information systems are installed within the timeframe identified by ED policy

In support of the ISO, ensures that actions are taken to respond and comply within specified timelines for any government-wide or ED-wide directed action items related to vulnerability patching

gaps: No mention of anti-malware or endpoint protection software deployment and management

recommendations: Develop a dedicated malware defense policy requiring deployment of anti-malware solutions on all enterprise endpoints, servers, and email gateways with automated updates
Implement application whitelisting or execution control policies to prevent unauthorized code and scripts from running on enterprise assets
Establish requirements for centralized anti-malware management with real-time monitoring, alerting, and reporting metrics
Define policies for automated scanning of removable media, downloaded files, and email attachments
Integrate malware defense metrics into the continuous monitoring strategy with defined KPIs for detection rates, response times, and coverage percentages
Include requirements for endpoint detection and response (EDR) capabilities with behavioral analysis to detect advanced threats

control_results.score_rationale: The policy contains only a brief, ad hoc mention of backups as a responsibility of System/Network/Website Administrators ('implements proper system backups') but lacks any formal data recovery practices, restoration procedures, recovery time objectives, or requirements for regular testing of backup and recovery processes.
evidence: Implements proper system backups and patch management processes;
gaps: No formal data recovery policy or procedures defined to restore enterprise assets to a pre-incident and trusted state
No requirement for regular testing of backup and recovery procedures
No defined recovery time objectives (RTO) or recovery point objectives (RPO)
No specification of backup scope, frequency, retention periods, or storage requirements (e.g., offsite, encrypted, immutable)
No defined roles and responsibilities specifically for data recovery beyond a general administrator duty

recommendations: Develop and publish a comprehensive Data Backup and Recovery Policy that defines backup scope, frequency, retention, and storage requirements for all in-scope enterprise assets
Establish and document Recovery Time Objectives (RTO) and Recovery Point Objectives (RPO) aligned with business impact analyses for each system classification
Mandate regular (at least annual) testing of backup restoration procedures with documented results, including full and partial recovery scenarios

Assign clear accountability for data recovery practices and integrate recovery metrics into continuous monitoring and reporting processes

evidence: Limits connections to publicly accessible Federal websites and web services to approved secure protocols.
